issues.description: Blocking read() loop has no timeout — a hung or stalled writer will hang the parent forever
issues.detail: The whole point of the original non-blocking + poll() dance was to be able to time out if the subprocess hangs. The author even brags about this in the PR description: 'Can timeout if subprocess hangs'. Then the patch turns around and, the moment one byte arrives, drops into an unbounded `while True: os.read()` with no poll, no timeout, no signal handling. If the writer writes 1 byte and then wedges (deadlock, GC pause, stuck on a network call before its final flush, paused under a debugger, SIGSTOP), the parent sits in a blocking read forever. You replaced an intermittent JSONDecodeError with a deterministic hang. That is not a fix, that is a worse bug with better marketing.

issues.description: check_process_exited + non-blocking EOF detection was deleted instead of being repaired
issues.detail: The removed block was the actual MacOS workaround: poll said nothing, read returned empty, and the code confirmed EOF by checking the writer process had exited. The new code deletes that path entirely and replaces it with `pass`. So on the first iteration, before any data has arrived, if poll times out and read returns empty, the loop just spins forever until data shows up or the BlockingIOError path triggers. If the subprocess dies before writing anything, you fall through to the post-loop `check_process_exited` and raise — fine — but if it dies after writing partial data on a platform where poll doesn't surface the hangup, you never enter the blocking branch and you never exit. The old logic existed for a documented reason; deleting the comment doesn't delete the reason.

issues.description: fcntl flag flip is not restored and not guarded — fd state leaks, errors are unhandled
issues.detail: `fcntl.fcntl(fifo_fd, F_SETFL, flags & ~O_NONBLOCK)` mutates the fd's flags and there is no try/finally to restore them. If this fd is owned by the caller or reused, you've silently changed its mode. fcntl can also raise OSError; the patch doesn't handle that. At minimum wrap the flip + blocking read in try/finally that restores the original flags, and decide explicitly whether fd ownership permits the mutation in the first place.

issues.description: BlockingIOError handler silently swallows the signal that used to terminate the loop
issues.detail: Old code: on BlockingIOError with content present, break — i.e. treat it as 'writer side closed, we're done.' New code: `pass`. So if the platform raises BlockingIOError instead of returning empty (which is exactly what the old comment said happens on some systems), the loop now busy-loops on poll forever instead of exiting. You kept the except clause but removed its only useful behavior. Either delete the except entirely or restore the break-on-content semantics; don't leave a no-op except as a trap for the next maintainer.

issues.description: Diagnosis cites a POSIX guarantee that doesn't apply the way the PR claims
issues.detail: The commit message says blocking read() returns 0 'ONLY after writer closes AND all kernel pipe buffers are drained — POSIX guaranteed.' That's true for a pipe with a single writer that has actually closed its end. It says nothing about a writer that hasn't flushed Python's userspace buffer yet, which is the actual root cause described in the PR (Python buffered I/O on the writer side). If the real bug is the writer not flushing before exit, the right fix is on the writer: flush + close, or use unbuffered/line-buffered I/O, or frame the messages with a length prefix. Switching the reader to blocking masks one race and adds another. State the actual invariant or fix the actual side.

issues.description: Two breaks, one `pass`, one dead-ish except — control flow is harder to read than the bug it fixes
issues.detail: The function now has: outer while, inner try, inner-inner while True with break, an else branch that does nothing, and an except that does nothing. A reader six months from now has to stare at this to figure out which loop the `break` exits. Refactor the post-first-byte path into a small helper (`_drain_blocking(fifo_fd)`) and let the outer loop's intent stay legible. Good taste: eliminate the special case, don't bury it under nested loops.

issues.description: No test accompanies a concurrency fix for a concurrency bug
issues.detail: This is a race-condition patch with a story about ~86KB truncation under concurrent deploys, and the diff contains zero tests. A fake writer that writes N bytes, closes, and a reader exercising both the poll-timeout-with-content and BlockingIOError-with-content paths would be a few dozen lines and would have caught the deleted-behavior regressions above. Without a test, the next refactor re-introduces the original bug and nobody notices until production.

review.summary: The diagnosis is plausible and the direction — switch to blocking reads once the stream is live — is defensible, but the patch as written trades an intermittent JSONDecodeError for a deterministic hang: the inner blocking loop has no timeout, no poll, and no way out if the writer stalls after its first byte. On top of that, the patch deletes the MacOS check_process_exited fallback and neuters the BlockingIOError branch to a bare `pass`, removing two of the three ways the old loop could terminate. The fcntl flag flip mutates fd state with no try/finally and no error handling. The real root cause described in the PR (writer-side Python buffering) arguably belongs on the writer, not papered over on the reader. NEEDS-WORK: restore a bounded wait in the blocking path, keep the process-exit EOF fallback, restore break-on-content for BlockingIOError, wrap the fcntl flip in try/finally, and add a test for stalled-writer and partial-content paths.
